notes: Thinner layers hide layer lines and improve curved surfaces, but print time grows almost in proportion.
Thicker layers print faster and bond more strongly between layers, but show visible steps.
layer_height.recommend: Recommended: 20% to 70% of the nozzle diameter.

notes: A thicker first layer tolerates an uneven bed and sticks more reliably.
A thinner first layer gives a smoother, more precise bottom surface but needs a well-leveled bed.
initial_layer_print_height.recommend: Recommended: 0.2 mm for a 0.4 mm nozzle.

notes: Wider lines are stronger and print faster, but lose fine detail and sharp corners.
Narrower lines resolve small features better but need more passes and take longer.
line_width.recommend: Recommended: 100% to 125% of the nozzle diameter.

notes: A wider first-layer line squishes into the bed for better adhesion.
Too wide a line can cause elephant foot or over-extrusion on the first layer.
initial_layer_line_width.recommend: Recommended: 120% to 150% of the nozzle diameter.

notes: Narrower outer walls give sharper details and a more accurate outer dimension.
Wider outer walls hide minor defects and print faster.
outer_wall_line_width.recommend: Recommended: 100% of the nozzle diameter, or slightly less for detail.

notes: Wider inner walls add strength and speed; narrower ones fit tight geometry better.
Inner walls are hidden, so width matters for strength rather than looks.
inner_wall_line_width.recommend: Recommended: 100% to 125% of the nozzle diameter.

notes: Narrower lines give a smoother, finer top surface at the cost of time.
Wider lines cover large flat areas faster but can leave visible ridges.
top_surface_line_width.recommend: Recommended: 90% to 100% of the nozzle diameter.

notes: Wider infill lines print much faster and add strength with fewer passes.
Very wide lines can bulge into the walls and need more cooling.
sparse_infill_line_width.recommend: Recommended: 120% to 150% of the nozzle diameter.

notes: Wider lines speed up solid layers hidden inside the part.
Narrower lines leave fewer gaps but take longer.
Wider support lines print faster and are sturdier.
Narrower lines give finer interface layers and cleaner support contact.
Aligned places seams in a neat line that is easy to sand or hide.
Random scatters seams so no single line is visible, but the surface looks slightly uneven.
Nearest and Back suit parts where one side must stay clean.
Offsets inner wall seams from the outer one so seam weak points do not stack.
Slightly improves strength and hides seams better on the outer wall.
A larger gap reduces seam blobs but can leave a small visible notch.
A smaller gap closes the loop better but risks a bulge at the seam.
seam_gap.recommend: Recommended: 10% of the nozzle diameter, or 0 on a well-tuned machine.

notes: Scarf seams ramp the wall in and out to make the seam almost invisible on smooth walls.
Works best on round or vertical walls and needs good pressure advance tuning.
Lower values start the ramp closer to the layer bottom, giving a gentler transition.
Higher values make the seam steeper and the overlap shorter.
seam_slope_start_height.recommend: Recommended: 0% to 50% of the layer height.

notes: Longer scarf ramps blend the seam better and reduce visible marks.
Very long ramps take more time and can bulge when flow is not tuned.
More steps make the ramp smoother but produce more G-code moves.
Fewer steps are lighter on the controller but give a coarser slope.
Lower values reduce material at the ramp to avoid bulging at the seam.
Raise it slightly if the seam shows a gap or an underfilled notch.
Moves the nozzle inward at the end of a wall loop to wipe off the seam blob.
Reduces seam zits at almost no time cost.
Wipes the nozzle into the part before the outer wall to hide the seam start.
Helps with outer-wall zits but can slightly shift the seam position.
Higher values merge tiny gaps and cracks in the model into one solid region.
Too high a value can fill in details that should stay open.
Lower values keep curves accurate but create larger G-code and slower slicing.
Higher values simplify the model, which can facet curves and drop fine detail.
Replaces many short segments with G2/G3 arcs, which shrinks G-code and smooths motion.
Requires firmware that supports arc commands; leave it off otherwise.
Positive values enlarge holes and negative values shrink them to correct printed size.
Print a test part with known holes and measure before adjusting.
Positive values grow the outer contour and negative values shrink it to correct dimensions.
Use it when parts consistently print larger or smaller than designed.
Shrinks the first layer inward to counter the flared bottom edge called elephant foot.
Too much leaves a visible groove at the base.
elefant_foot_compensation.recommend: Recommended: 0.1 mm to 0.3 mm, only if elephant foot appears.

notes: Adjusts wall spacing so the outer surface matches the model dimensions more closely.
Improves dimensional accuracy for parts that must fit together.
Adjusts the last layer heights so the print reaches the exact model height.
May produce a slightly thinner top layer instead of an off-height part.
Converts round holes to polygons whose flats sit inside the true circle, so printed holes match the nominal diameter.
Improves fit for bolts and pins in small holes.
Ironing passes a hot, low-flow nozzle over the top surface to melt and flatten it.
Gives a glossy, smooth top at the cost of extra print time.
Top surfaces only is usually enough; use Topmost only for the final layer.
Higher flow fills tiny gaps better but can leave excess material and rough streaks.
Lower flow gives a lighter polish and less risk of blobs.
Smaller spacing gives a smoother finish but increases ironing time.
Larger spacing is faster but may leave ridges between passes.
Slower ironing melts the surface more evenly.
Very high speeds leave streaks and do little smoothing.
Arachne varies line width to fill thin and tapered walls without gaps, giving stronger parts.
Classic keeps constant line width and is more predictable and slightly faster to slice.
Inner-then-outer hides inner-wall flaws and is more accurate for overhangs.
Outer-then-inner gives cleaner outer surfaces but can show inner-wall pressure marks.
Inner-outer-inner balances the two for tight dimensional accuracy.
Scales extrusion for the whole process on top of the filament flow ratio.
Use small steps only; tune the filament flow ratio first.
Prints a single wall on the first layer so more of the layer is solid infill.
Improves bed adhesion and first-layer surface quality on thin parts.
Uses one wall on top surface layers to leave more room for top infill.
Gives a smoother top finish but slightly weaker top edges.
Routes travel moves around walls to avoid crossing them and leaving marks.
Can lengthen travel paths and add time on complex parts.
Sets how far a travel may detour to avoid crossing walls.
Higher values avoid more crossings but lengthen travel.
max_travel_detour_distance.recommend: Recommended: 0 for no limit, or about 5 mm to 10 mm.

notes: Lower flow thins the bridge strand so it sags less.
Too low causes gaps and snapped strands; too high causes sagging.
Prints bridges with round, full-nozzle-diameter strands that span gaps more reliably.
Improves bridge strength but may leave a rougher underside.
Detects overhanging walls and slows them down so they print cleanly.
Required for the overhang speed and fan settings to apply.
Modifies the model slope so overhangs print without supports.
Changes the geometry slightly, so avoid it on precision parts.
Adds extra wall passes over overhangs to build a better base for the next layer.
Raises print time and material on parts with many overhangs.
Alternates wall direction on overhang layers so curled edges are pushed back inward.
Works best with strong cooling on the overhang.
More walls make the part stronger and stiffer than extra infill does.
Each extra wall adds print time and material.
wall_loops.recommend: Recommended: 2 to 4 walls for functional parts.

notes: Adds an extra wall on every other layer to fill gaps between infill and walls.
Improves strength and top surface support at a small time cost.
Detects walls thinner than two lines and prints them as a single pass.
Prevents gaps and missing thin features but may add slight extrusion variance.
More top layers give a stronger, more sealed top and better coverage over sparse infill.
Each extra layer adds print time.
top_shell_layers.recommend: Recommended: 4 to 6 layers at 0.2 mm layer height.

notes: Sets a minimum top thickness; the slicer uses whichever is greater, this or the layer count.
Mostly useful at very thin layer heights, where the layer count alone is too thin.
Monotonic gives the smoothest look by keeping all lines in one direction.
Concentric and Hilbert curve suit decorative tops but may leave seams or take longer.
More bottom layers make the base stronger and give better bed contact.
Each extra layer adds print time and material.
bottom_shell_layers.recommend: Recommended: 3 to 5 layers at 0.2 mm layer height.

notes: Sets a minimum bottom thickness, overriding the layer count when it is greater.
Useful at thin layer heights, where a few layers are not enough.
Controls the fill pattern of the visible bottom surface.
Monotonic gives a cleaner bottom finish; rectilinear prints faster.
Higher density adds strength and top support but increases time, weight and material.
Most strength comes from walls; density above 40% rarely pays off.
sparse_infill_density.recommend: Recommended: 10% to 20% for decorative parts, 25% to 40% for functional parts.

notes: Grid and cubic give strong, uniform support; lines and zig-zag print faster.
Gyroid is isotropic but slower to slice; lightning saves the most material on display parts.
Sets the angle of the infill lines in the XY plane.
Aligning infill to the load direction can improve strength.
Sets how far infill lines may extend along the wall to anchor to it.
Longer anchors improve adhesion but add extrusion on the wall.
Caps the anchor length so short infill lines are not connected to long extra segments.
Lower values give cleaner infill but weaker bonding to walls.
More overlap bonds infill to walls better but can show through the outer wall.
Less overlap prevents bulges and ghosting on thin walls.
More overlap bonds skin to walls better but can cause bulges at edges.
Less overlap gives cleaner edges with slightly weaker bonding.
Forces a bridge direction instead of letting the slicer choose.
Align it to span the shortest gap for the best support.
Prints infill every few layers using thicker lines, saving time.
Reduces detail inside the part; walls and top layers are unchanged.
Adds solid infill near sloped surfaces to keep the shell thick.
Prevents thin spots and pillowing, at some extra material.
Areas smaller than this get solid infill instead of sparse infill.
Raising it removes tiny sparse pockets that print poorly.
Chooses where thin gaps are filled: everywhere, only between walls, or nowhere.
Filling gaps adds strength but may leave visible lines on thin features.
Slower first layers stick better and tolerate a less-perfect bed.
Raising it saves little time and risks poor adhesion.
Controls infill speed on the first layer only.
Raising it saves time on large parts, but keep it moderate for adhesion.
Faster travel on the first layer reduces oozing time over the bed.
Too fast can knock loose parts that have not stuck yet.
Number of initial layers printed at a ramped-up speed rather than full speed.
Higher values give a gentler transition from first layer to normal speed.
Slower outer walls improve surface quality and dimensional accuracy.
Faster outer walls save time but show ringing and layer inconsistency.
outer_wall_speed.recommend: Recommended: 40% to 60% of the inner wall speed.

notes: Inner walls are hidden, so they can run faster than the outer wall to save time.
Too fast can hurt layer bonding and strength.
Slows small holes and features, which cool too little and overheat at normal speed.
Improves accuracy on tiny circles.
Infill is hidden, so it can run fast, limited mainly by flow rate and vibration.
Too fast risks under-extrusion and weak infill.
Controls the speed of solid layers hidden inside the part.
Lower speeds support top layers better; higher speeds save time.
Slower top surfaces give a smoother finish with fewer ridges.
Higher speeds save time but can leave roughness.
Faster supports save time since their quality matters little.
Too fast can make supports fragile and break during printing.
Slower interfaces give a smoother surface under the supported part.
Raising it saves time but may roughen the supported surface.
Slows walls over overhangs by the overhang percentage so the extrusion cools and holds shape.
Improves overhang quality at the cost of print time.
Slower bridges sag less and keep strands tight, given good cooling.
Faster bridges stretch strands thin and may snap them.
Controls the speed of bridges over sparse infill, which are usually short.
Slower values reduce sagging into the infill.
Faster travel cuts time and ooze, as the nozzle spends less time over the print.
Too fast causes vibration, skipped steps or ringing marks.
travel_speed.recommend: Recommended: 150 mm/s to 500 mm/s, depending on the printer.

notes: Lower acceleration reduces ringing and improves quality but increases print time.
Higher acceleration saves time on large, simple parts.
A low value on outer walls reduces ringing and keeps edges sharp.
Costs time only on visible surfaces.
Inner walls can accelerate harder than the outer wall since they are not visible.
Too high may affect outer wall quality through vibration.
Lower acceleration keeps bridge strands straighter and avoids breaking them.
Higher acceleration speeds up hidden infill but shakes the printer.
Keep it within what the machine can handle without marking the walls.
Higher acceleration shortens solid-layer time inside the part.
A low value on the first layer improves adhesion and avoids dislodging the part.
A low value on top surfaces reduces ringing and gives a smoother finish.
Higher travel acceleration shortens non-printing moves.
Too high can shake the printer and cause layer shifts.
Higher values allow faster cornering but cause bulging and ringing at corners.
Lower values slow corners for cleaner edges.
Higher jerk allows quicker direction changes but increases vibration and ringing.
Lower jerk slows corners and gives cleaner walls.
A lower value on outer walls reduces corner artifacts and ringing.
Smooths sudden changes in extrusion rate so flow ramps up and down gradually.
Reduces pressure artifacts at speed changes; heavy smoothing can slow some moves.
Adds temporary structures under overhangs so they do not droop or collapse.
Costs time and material and leaves marks where supports touch the part.
enable_support.recommend: Recommended: on for overhangs steeper than about 45 degrees.

notes: Normal supports are fast and reliable on simple shapes.
Tree supports use less material and leave fewer marks on organic models.
Controls how the support structure is built, trading stability against material and removal effort.
Snug and slim styles save material; grid and default styles are sturdier.
Overhangs steeper than this angle get supports; a lower value adds more support.
Raise it to save supports on surfaces that print fine unsupported.
Limits supports to those starting on the bed, avoiding supports on the part itself.
Leaves some overhangs unsupported when there is no clear path to the bed.
A larger gap makes supports easier to remove but roughens the overhang underside.
A smaller gap gives a better finish but supports can fuse to the part.
Sets the gap where supports rest on the part from below.
Larger values ease removal; smaller values give firmer bases.
Rectilinear is fast and easy to remove; honeycomb is sturdier but uses more material.
Lightning is the lightest, for tall or simple supports.
Wider spacing saves material and time but gives less support for the layers above.
Tighter spacing holds up wider overhangs and is harder to remove.
More interface layers give a smoother overhang surface and easier removal.
Each layer adds print time and material.
Tighter spacing gives a denser, smoother contact surface but sticks harder to the part.
Wider spacing breaks away more easily but leaves a rougher underside.
A larger gap keeps supports from fusing to walls but weakens side support.
A smaller gap holds the part better but is harder to remove.
Skips supports under bridges that are short enough to span unaided.
Saves material but long or heavy bridges may sag.
A larger angle lets branches lean further and reach more areas.
Smaller angles are more stable and less likely to bend.
Thicker branches are sturdier but use more material and are harder to remove.
Thin branches save material but can wobble on tall supports.
A smaller tip leaves less of a mark on the part.
A larger tip supports the surface more firmly but is harder to clean off.
A raft is a printed base under the part that improves adhesion and evens out the first layer.
Costs time and material, and the underside of the part ends up rougher.
A larger gap makes the raft easier to peel off but roughens the underside.
A smaller gap fuses better and can make removal difficult.
Prints a tower to purge and prime the nozzle after each filament change.
Needed for clean color changes; adds time and material.
A wider tower is more stable and gives more room for purging.
A narrower tower saves material but may wobble when tall.
Sets the volume extruded to prime the nozzle after a change.
Too little leaves old color in the first strokes; too much wastes filament.
Purges old filament into the infill of the current object instead of the tower.
Cuts waste, but the infill may show the old color through thin walls.
Purges into other objects on the plate to reduce waste.
Use on objects that are not visible or do not mind color bleed.
Purges into the support structures, which are discarded anyway.
Reduces waste with no impact on the final part.
Lowers the temperature of idle tools during multi-tool prints to reduce oozing.
Needs extra heating time before each tool change.
Adds interlocking beams where two materials meet to strengthen their bond.
Works best with materials that do not adhere well to each other.
More loops purge more material and make a larger test outline.
Set 0 to disable the skirt.
A larger distance keeps the skirt clear of the part, useful when it must be removed.
A smaller distance primes closer to the first-layer start but may merge with a brim.
Number of layers printed for the skirt.
Taller skirts act as a draft shield but waste material.
skirt_height.recommend: Recommended: 1 layer, or more for a draft shield.

notes: Builds a wall around the object to protect it from drafts and trap warmth.
Helps ABS and ASA warp less, but adds time and material.
A brim widens the first layer to hold the part down and prevent warping.
Outer brim sits outside the part; inner brim also fills inside holes; brim ears only touch sharp corners.
A wider brim holds the part more firmly but is harder to remove and wastes material.
Narrow brims suit small contact areas with a good bed.
A small gap makes the brim easier to peel off the part.
A gap too large reduces how well the brim holds the part.
By layer prints all objects layer by layer and is faster.
By object finishes one object at a time but needs enough clearance to avoid collisions.
Prints the outer wall as one continuous spiral, avoiding seams and Z jumps.
Only for single-wall vases; no infill, top-layer details or travel moves are used.
Pauses at each layer to take a photo from a fixed toolhead position.
Traditional mode adds time per layer; smooth mode keeps the toolhead moving and needs a prime tower.
Adds random jitter to the outer wall for a rough, textured finish that hides layer lines.
Gives better grip but changes the part dimensions slightly.
Larger values give a rougher texture and a bigger dimensional change.
Smaller values give subtle texture.
A larger distance gives coarser fuzz with fewer moves.
A smaller distance gives finer fuzz but creates more G-code.
Skips retractions when travelling inside infill to save time.
Can leave faint strings that stay hidden inside the part.
Lets the printer skip a failed object during the print.
Needs firmware support and adds object labels to the G-code.
Adds object labels to the G-code for firmware features such as object cancellation.
Has no effect on print quality.
Adds explanatory comments to the G-code.
Makes files larger; useful for debugging, not needed for printing.
Prints wave-shaped extrusions across overhangs to bridge steep angles without support.
Works best on short spans with strong part cooling and tuned flow.
Test on a small part first, since results depend on material and cooling.
Replaces bridge detection with solid infill when wave overhangs are on.
Leave it off to keep simple flat spans as normal bridges.
Smaller spacing makes a denser, stronger wave surface but uses more time and heat.
Larger spacing prints faster but may leave gaps between lines.
Slower speeds give each bead more time to cool and hold shape in the air.
Faster speeds risk sagging and snapped strands.
Higher fan speed solidifies wave beads faster and reduces sagging.
Too strong airflow can cool the layer below too much and hurt bonding.
Adds a pause when a wave region would finish too quickly, giving it time to solidify.
Raise it if waves droop; it adds print time.
Number of solid layers placed above wave regions to back the cantilever.
More layers add strength and rigidity but use more time and material.
Sets the plastic volume per millimetre of wave line, independent of layer height.
Raise it for stronger beads, lower it if lines sag or merge.
Selects the build plate type, which sets the bed temperatures from the filament profile.
Choose the plate that matches the one installed on the printer.
The slicer uses it to convert flow into extrusion length, so a wrong value over- or under-extrudes.
Measure the actual filament at several points and use the average.
Used only to estimate part weight in the statistics.
Does not change the print itself.
Used only to estimate print cost per kilogram of filament.
Does not change the print itself.
Scales extrusion to compensate for material and nozzle differences.
Raise it if walls look thin or gappy; lower it if walls bulge or surfaces look rough.
filament_flow_ratio.recommend: Recommended: calibrate with a flow test, usually between 0.94 and 1.05.

notes: Compensates for filament pressure lag, sharpening corners and evening out line width.
Needs a calibrated value for each filament and nozzle.
Too low leaves bulging corners and gaps after speed changes; too high causes thin or gappy corners.
Calibrate it with a pressure advance test pattern for each filament.
Adjusts pressure advance with flow rate and acceleration instead of using one fixed value.
Needs a calibrated model, otherwise results can be worse than a fixed value.
Higher temperature improves layer bonding and flow but increases stringing and oozing.
Lower temperature reduces stringing and improves overhangs but can cause weak layers or under-extrusion.
nozzle_temperature.recommend: Recommended: within the filament's printable range, for example 200 C to 230 C for PLA.

notes: A slightly hotter first layer improves adhesion to the bed.
Too hot can cause elephant foot or stringing at the start.
A hotter bed improves adhesion and reduces warping on high-shrink materials.
Too hot softens the first layers and can cause elephant foot.
hot_plate_temp.recommend: Recommended: 55 C to 65 C for PLA, 70 C to 90 C for PETG, 90 C to 110 C for ABS.

notes: Sets the bed temperature for the first layer only.
A slightly higher value helps adhesion before dropping to the normal bed temperature.
Caps flow so the hotend is not asked to melt more plastic than it can.
Too high causes under-extrusion; too low slows prints unnecessarily.
filament_max_volumetric_speed.recommend: Recommended: 12 mm3/s for PLA on a standard hotend; calibrate for your setup.

notes: Scales the model to offset the material's cooling shrinkage.
Matters for ABS, ASA and nylon; keep it 100% for low-shrink materials.
The minimum part cooling fan speed used when layers are slow enough.
Lower values keep layers warmer and bond better; higher values improve detail.
The maximum part cooling fan speed, reached on short layers.
Higher speeds improve overhangs and bridges but can weaken layer bonding.
Keeps the fan off for the first layers so they stay warm and stick.
Too few layers risk lifting corners; too many can hurt early overhangs.
Ramps the fan up gradually until it reaches full speed at this layer.
Useful for materials that need a gentle transition from first layers.
Layers that take less than this many seconds get more cooling.
Raise it for small parts that overheat; leave it lower for large parts.
Slows layers that print faster than this time, giving each layer time to cool.
Improves small parts and tips, at the cost of longer print time.
The lowest speed layer cooling is allowed to slow the print to.
Too low causes blobs from heat build-up; too high gives less cooling benefit.
Boosts the fan on overhangs and bridges to solidify them quickly.
Raise it if overhangs curl or droop.
Runs the auxiliary fan to move more air over the part.
Helps PLA and bridging; disable it for ABS and ASA to avoid warping.
Sets a target chamber temperature to reduce warping and improve layer bonding.
Useful for ABS, ASA and nylon; leave it off for PLA, which softens in a hot chamber.
Determines default temperatures and compatibility checks for mixed prints.
Set the correct type so incompatible materials are flagged in multi-material prints.
Marks the material as dissolvable, such as PVA, so it can be used for supports.
Soluble materials are often moisture sensitive and need dry storage.
Marks the filament as a support material.
Lets the slicer assign it to support structures and use its dedicated settings.
Runs G-code each time this filament is loaded for printing.
Use it for filament-specific commands such as pressure advance.
Runs G-code each time this filament finishes or is unloaded.
Use it for cleanup commands specific to this filament.
Must match the installed nozzle, as line widths and flow are derived from it.
A wrong value gives incorrect extrusion and layer height limits.
Defines the bed shape the slicer can place objects on.
Must match the real bed, otherwise objects may be placed out of reach.
Maximum object height the printer can reach.
Prevents slicing models taller than the printer can build.
Marks parts of the bed where nothing should be printed, such as clips.
Objects are kept out of these zones when arranging.
Shifts all Z positions to compensate for nozzle-to-bed distance.
Use small steps; adjust only if the first layer is consistently too high or too low.
Selects the firmware dialect for G-code commands.
A wrong flavor can break temperature, retraction or acceleration commands.
Uses relative extruder moves, which avoids precision loss on long prints.
Required by some firmware; leave on if your printer supports it.
Lets the firmware handle retraction with G10 and G11 instead of slicer-set moves.
Needs firmware support and tuning; settings come from the firmware.
Longer retraction reduces stringing but risks clogs and extruder wear.
Direct drive usually needs 0.5 mm to 2 mm; Bowden setups need more.
retraction_length.recommend: Recommended: 0.5 mm to 1 mm for direct drive, 3 mm to 6 mm for Bowden.

notes: Faster retraction pulls the filament back before it oozes.
Too fast can grind the filament; too slow lets plastic ooze.
Travel moves shorter than this skip retraction.
Raising it saves time but may leave strings on short hops.
Lifts the nozzle during travel to avoid scraping the print.
Reduces collisions but adds time and can increase stringing.
z_hop.recommend: Recommended: 0.2 mm to 0.4 mm, or 0 to disable.

notes: Retracts before moving to the next layer to avoid a blob at the layer change.
Minor time cost; helps hide the seam.
Moves the nozzle along the path during retraction to wipe ooze off the tip.
Reduces blobs and strings, with a small time cost.
Retracts part of the length before wiping so the tip is clean as it moves.
Lower values wipe with more pressure; higher values retract earlier.
Caps the acceleration the printer may use on this axis.
Set it to what the firmware and frame handle without skipping steps or ringing.
Caps the speed the printer may use on this axis.
Higher limits only help if the motors and frame can sustain them.
Runs once before printing, to home, heat and prepare the printer.
Errors here can ruin every print, so test changes on a short print.
Runs after the print, to cool down, park the head and turn off heaters.
Make sure it turns off heaters and fans to keep the printer safe.
Runs before every layer change.
Adds a command per layer, so keep it short to avoid slowing the print.
Runs at every layer change, after the move to the new layer.
Commonly used for timelapse triggers or progress commands.
Runs during filament changes to unload and load the material.
Required for multi-material setups; errors can cause jams.
Runs when a pause is inserted in the print.
Use it to park the head and beep or notify.
Radius around the nozzle used to avoid collisions in print-by-object mode.
Larger values leave more space between objects but reduce how many fit.
Height at which the gantry clears when printing object by object.
Taller objects than this cannot be printed one after another.
Records nozzle hardness for abrasive filament warnings.
Does not change the print itself.
Enables belt-printer mode, with a tilted slicing plane and transformed G-code coordinates.
Only for belt printers; leave it off on regular printers.
Sets the preview image sizes embedded in the G-code.
Use only sizes your printer's screen supports.
Stops the slicer from emitting remaining-time commands.
Use it if your firmware does not understand M73 and shows errors.
Starts the fan earlier so it reaches the target speed when needed.
Compensates for fan spin-up lag on printers with slow fans.
Runs the fan at full power briefly before the target speed to get it spinning.
Useful for fans that stall at low PWM.
Adds a margin around the print area for adaptive bed mesh probing.
Larger margins probe more of the bed and take longer.
Free text stored with the printer profile.
Used by some profiles to carry flags or hints, so edit it carefully.
Free text stored with the filament profile.
Use it for reminders such as drying time or tuning results.
Free text stored with the process profile.
Use it to record what the profile is for.
